title: Present needs and future opportunities

blocks.heading: Present needs and future opportunities
blocks.text: Sustainable development is development that meets present needs without undermining future generations' ability to meet their own needs. Present needs include adequate food, water, shelter and opportunities to earn a living. Future generations also need a functioning environment and usable resources. The idea connects these needs: keeping people poor is not a satisfactory way to protect a resource, and meeting needs today by destroying tomorrow's productive base is not a lasting solution.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: A water-use decision
blocks.text: Consider an invented settlement whose shared water source supports households and a small irrigated garden. During a dry period, unrestricted garden pumping leaves too little water for households and risks exhausting the available supply. A locally agreed allocation could reserve essential household water, limit pumping to a monitored amount and reduce avoidable losses from leaking pipes. The proposal addresses a present need without assuming that unlimited extraction can continue. Its success depends on a realistic water assessment, workable rules and maintenance. Installing a pump alone does not show that the water use is sustainable.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Ask what lasts and who benefits
blocks.text: A proposal should identify the need it meets, the resource or condition it depends on and how that resource will remain usable. Benefits also need to reach the people whose needs are being discussed. A project that protects water while excluding households from essential access leaves an important development problem unresolved. Explain the trade-off with a concrete mechanism rather than labelling an activity sustainable because it sounds environmentally friendly.

blocks.heading: Connect to development and production
blocks.text: Topic 1.1 explains the economic, social, political and environmental dimensions. Topic 3.1 explains production and resource use. Sustainability asks whether improvements in those dimensions can continue while resources and living conditions are protected.

blocks.heading: Sustainable Development Goals
blocks.text: The United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) organise international development ambitions for 2030. The saved 2022 examination figure shows examples including No Poverty, Zero Hunger, Good Health and Well-being, Clean Water and Sanitation, Decent Work and Economic Growth, and Responsible Consumption and Production. The syllabus specifically names SDG 12. Sustainable development can be considered through linked economic, social and environmental pillars; a goal may contribute to more than one, so do not force every goal into only one pillar. Progress in one area can help another, but trade-offs still need a judgement about present and future needs.
